implementation_notes: The Java persistence standard absorbs the mapper: an @ManyToOne field with @JoinColumn(name = "CUSTOMER_ID", nullable = false) owns the foreign key column, the inverse @OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer") reads the same association, and fetch = FetchType.LAZY defers resolving the key to the referenced entity. Providers such as Hibernate keep one instance per row in the session identity map and write the key on flush, so the association appears as a plain object reference. The classic hand-written mapper is still justified for legacy or unconstrained schemas and for hot queries where the provider's SQL is not acceptable.
pitfalls: @ManyToOne defaults to EAGER: without fetch = LAZY every order load drags a customer in, and eager chains turn into a join explosion.
The owning side is the one with the FK column; mapping only the @OneToMany side (or both without mappedBy) creates two overlapping associations or an unwanted join table.
equals/hashCode on a generated id breaks in sets before flush and lazy proxies defeat identity comparison - compare keys, not proxies.

variants.name: Hand-written JDBC mapper with a session identity map
variants.idiom_name: ResultSet key read + HashMap identity map + setLong write-back
variants.implementation_notes: Without a provider the mapper is explicit code: read the key with ResultSet.getLong("customer_id"), resolve it through a per-session identity map (HashMap<Long, Customer>), write it back with setLong when the order is saved. You keep the SQL and the domain classes stay free of annotations; you also own ordering, caching and cycle handling, which is exactly what the provider would have done for you.
pitfalls: The identity map must be scoped to a session; a static map keeps stale customers alive and leaks memory in a long-running server.
Prepared statements and ResultSets must be closed on every path - a leaked cursor is the classic failure of hand-written JDBC mappers.
Long ids and nullable keys need explicit handling (getLong returns 0 for NULL): use wasNull() so a missing reference does not become customer 0.
